strengths: NC-OOD offers a practical, simple post-hoc detector. Equation (5) combines classifier-weight alignment with feature magnitude, requiring only a global feature mean beyond the trained classifier. Its small storage requirements and inexpensive scoring make it potentially useful for computer vision deployment.

The evaluation covers three ID datasets, ResNet and DenseNet architectures, and cross-entropy and supervised contrastive training. Table 1 reports strong average AUROC: 95.36 versus 94.92 for KNN on CIFAR-10, and 94.15 versus 93.40 for DICE+ReAct on ImageNet.

The component ablations provide meaningful evidence for the combined score. On ImageNet, Table 4 reports 94.15 AUROC for NCScore versus 88.69 for pScore and 87.08 for the L1 norm alone. Under supervised contrastive training, average FPR95 improves from 11.61 for KNN+ to 9.84 for NC-OOD.

The scoring equations and geometric illustration communicate the method clearly. Selecting alpha using synthetic Gaussian noise provides a practical validation protocol without requiring examples from the evaluated OOD datasets. Reporting both AUROC and FPR95, including detailed appendix results, helps assess performance beyond a single summary metric.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is not established as stated. Equation (3) proves, at most, normalized alignment; obtaining the unnormalized convergence in Equation (1) requires additional control of class-mean norms. For example, two balanced classes with means ±(t,1), weights ±(1,0), and zero within-class variance satisfy NC1 and NC3, yet the Equation (1) residual norm approaches 1. The angular motivation remains plausible, but the claimed theorem needs stronger assumptions or a weaker conclusion.

The distinctive contribution of neural collapse is insufficiently isolated. Training-feature/weight alignment follows closely from the existing NC properties, while similarity-plus-magnitude scoring already appears in CSI. The manuscript does not quantify collapse in the evaluated networks or compare weight directions against empirical class-mean directions. Comparisons with closely relevant alternatives such as MaxLogit and ViM are also absent. Consequently, the evidence establishes a useful scoring rule more clearly than a new explanation of OOD separation.

The evidence supports broad competitiveness more strongly than consistent superiority. Table 3 reports lower average AUROC than KNN on DenseNet/CIFAR-10 and DICE+ReAct on DenseNet/CIFAR-100. More consequentially, Table 10 reports CIFAR-100 FPR95 of 62.62 for NC-OOD versus 47.36 for KNN. The smaller improvements, including the 0.15-point contrastive AUROC gain, have no uncertainty estimates establishing their robustness.

Several reporting inconsistencies affect interpretation. Section 4.4.1 claims pScore outperforms KNN across all ImageNet OOD sets, but Texture AUROC is 91.86 versus 97.07. In Table 10, the listed ReAct+DICE FPR95 values average approximately 45.00, not 76.45; Mahalanobis AUROC averages approximately 85.03, not 82.73. The former changes the baseline ranking. These numerical issues matter more than the readily correctable table-reference and caption errors.

Reproducibility and sensitivity analysis remain incomplete. The manuscript does not specify KNN's k, the supervised-contrastive classifier-head training procedure, or the Gaussian validation set size and selection metric. The norm ablations also do not clearly separate norm choice from effective weighting across differently scaled norms, and efficiency claims lack measured timings. Overall, the useful method and substantial component gains place the paper near acceptance, but unresolved theoretical correctness and contribution-attribution concerns keep the recommendation borderline.
